strengths: Novel conceptual contribution: Using adversarial learning to match intermediate marginal distributions in interpolant learning is genuinely innovative and well-motivated, clearly distinguished from pointwise matching in prior work
Solid theoretical foundations with rigorous uniqueness theorems (2.1 and 2.2) providing principled justification for regularizer design
Compelling results on targeted problems: Clear demonstration of advantages on synthetic knot data (1,200 time steps) and cell tracking where geometric variation over time is significant
Novel application domain: First application of flow matching to spatial transcriptomics coordinate inference with ~10% improvement over baselines
Strong handling of challenging settings: Demonstrates scalability to hundreds of marginal distributions and robustness to noisy, subsampled data where competing methods fail
Comprehensive experimental validation: Four diverse experiments with multiple baselines, visual comparisons, and quantitative metrics with extensive implementation details in appendix
Clear and well-structured presentation effectively motivating the problem and explaining limitations of prior approaches
weaknesses: Underperformance on standard trajectory inference benchmarks undermines practical impact: scRNA-seq experiments show 14-15% worse performance than OT-MFM on Tables 1-2, raising questions about method applicability to the primary domain

Loose theoretical-practical connection: Uniqueness theorems guarantee minimizers of regularized problems but don't address convergence of alternating GAN optimization; constraint satisfaction is only approximate with no quantified approximation error analysis

GAN training stability and reproducibility concerns: Different regularizers/hyperparameters used across experiments without systematic justification; critical details (Gaussian noise on time inputs) buried in appendix; no ablation on regularization weight λ
Limited spatial transcriptomics validation: Only one dataset tested with heavy manual preprocessing (H&E alignment); cannot assess generalization across platforms, tissues, or cancer types

Insufficient ablation studies: No direct comparison of three regularizers on same data; no sensitivity analysis for λ or coupling choice; missing analysis of whether full adversarial training is necessary
Unexplained performance trade-off: Authors acknowledge adversarial training makes scRNA-seq performance worse than OT-MFM but provide no principled solution or guidance on method selection
Missing computational cost analysis: No comparison of computational overhead from training three networks (generator, discriminator, flow matching) versus single-network baselines

strengths: Novel approach to interpolant learning using adversarial objectives to match intermediate marginals in distribution sense, clearly distinguishing from prior pointwise-matching methods
Solid theoretical contributions: Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 establish uniqueness of interpolants under specific regularization schemes with rigorous proofs
Clear motivation: identifies concrete limitations of existing methods (e.g., OT-MFM's time-independent metric failing when data geometry varies with time)
Demonstrates versatility across multiple domains (synthetic, cell tracking, scRNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics)
Strong performance on synthetic knot experiment (§4.1) with favorable geometry, clearly outperforming baselines
weaknesses: Empirical results are mixed and unconvincing: scRNA-seq results (Tables 1-2) are on par with or worse than OT-MFM, contradicting the paper's central claims; authors acknowledge adversarial training structurally makes it difficult to outperform baselines

Cell tracking evaluation (§4.2) relies entirely on visual inspection with explicit statement 'we constrained the analysis here to visual evaluations'—quantitative metrics are absent and essential for a top-tier venue

GAN training challenges inadequately addressed: method requires R3GAN for scRNA-seq (different algorithm suggesting base method fragility), extensive hyperparameter tuning varies across experiments (learning rates, noise injection, pretraining), and no ablation studies demonstrate training stability improvements

Core contribution not convincingly demonstrated: distribution-matching superiority shown only on toy synthetic problem and visual-only cell tracking; scRNA-seq results contradict the claimed advantage, indicating the benefit is unclear in realistic settings

Limited experimental scope: all real-data experiments use K≤5 (small marginal counts); large-K capability claimed for K=1,200 synthetic knot but K=115 cell tracking lacks quantitative evaluation; single dataset for spatial transcriptomics

Reproducibility severely compromised: no code availability, hyperparameters vary significantly across experiments (appendix D.1-D.4), complex manual preprocessing for ST data (BigWarp alignment), baselines reimplemented rather than using official code risking unfair comparison
Incomplete evaluation methodology: no computational cost analysis despite sequential training of G_φ, D_γ, u_θ; no statistical significance testing; missing comparison with Lee et al. (2025)

Technical concerns: Equation (5) parametrization unexplained; 'smooth time-input' via noise injection (0.001 std) appears to be a practical hack rather than principled solution; regularization weight λ requires tuning with no guidance for new applications; no convergence guarantees for the min-max adversarial problem

strengths: Novel technical approach: Adversarial learning to match intermediate marginals in distribution (rather than pointwise) is well-motivated and addresses real limitations of prior methods on time-varying geometries
Theoretical contributions: Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 provide uniqueness guarantees for proposed regularizers with sound proofs

Strong empirical results on important applications: Spatial transcriptomics shows significant improvements (EMD 98.91 vs 109.76-183.88 for baselines); cell tracking demonstrates clear superiority over alternatives
Comprehensive and diverse experiments: Synthetic knot (1,200 marginals), cell tracking with real data, multiple scRNA-seq datasets, and novel spatial transcriptomics application
Clear presentation and effective visualizations: Figures 2-4 clearly convey methodological differences and advantages
Practical flexibility: Three regularizer options (Eqs. 9, 11, 14) provide different tradeoffs for practitioners
Well-designed experiments that address specific limitations of baselines (e.g., time-varying geometry, non-smooth interpolants)
weaknesses: Mixed empirical performance: Comparable or worse results than OT-MFM on standard scRNA-seq benchmarks (Tables 1-2), limiting general applicability. Authors acknowledge distributional matching trades off pointwise accuracy

GAN training stability inadequately addressed: Heavy reliance on regularizers and variant objectives (R3GAN); requires pretraining, noise injection, and time smoothing. No systematic analysis of failure modes or when training diverges

Missing convergence analysis: Uniqueness theorems establish optimality conditions but provide no convergence guarantees for the adversarial training procedure. Formal connection between GAN loss (Eq. 7) and constraint satisfaction (Eq. 6) is absent

Insufficient hyperparameter guidance: Method requires extensive tuning (λ, noise levels, learning rates, network architectures) that varies significantly across datasets. Different regularizers used for different experiments with no ablation studies. Practitioners would struggle to apply to new problems

Weak statistical validation: Spatial transcriptomics results (N=5 runs) show error bar overlap between ALI-CFM and OT-MMFM; no significance tests. Cell tracking only has qualitative visual evaluation (Section 4.2)

Practical complexity underestimated: Two-stage training, careful GAN loss balancing, and scattered critical implementation details (appendix D) suggest method is difficult to apply. No computational cost or runtime comparisons provided

Limited characterization of when method works: No principled guidance on task/data properties where ALI-CFM outperforms alternatives. Synthetic knot designed to favor method's strengths (time-varying geometry)
ST preprocessing introduces subjectivity: Manual image alignment via BigWarp (Appendix C) undermines robustness claims; sensitivity to alignment quality unexplored
Incomplete high-dimensional comparisons: Authors state OT-MMFM 'poorly scales' but only ran baseline on 5D scRNA-seq, not 50D/100D where ALI-CFM is evaluated

strengths: Novel combination of adversarial training and flow matching for learning smooth interpolants in distribution rather than pointwise
Theoretical contributions with uniqueness theorems (2.1, 2.2) providing mathematical grounding
Impressive scalability demonstrated on 1,200 marginal distributions with sparse sampling
Strong experimental results on spatial transcriptomics tumor coordinate inference (Table 3: 98.91±2.03 vs 109.76 for OT-CFM)
Comprehensive experiments across diverse applications (synthetic knot, cell tracking, scRNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics)
Clear visual evidence of smoother learned interpolants compared to piecewise linear/cubic spline methods (Figure 8)
Well-structured methodology with clear algorithm descriptions (Algorithms 1-2)
Robustness to noisy data demonstrated in cell tracking experiments
weaknesses: Inconsistent performance on standard benchmarks: achieves 'on par' results with OT-MFM on single-cell trajectory inference (Tables 1-2), undermining claims of general superiority; improvements not statistically significant in some cases
GAN training stability and convergence not systematically analyzed; no comparison of training curves; high sensitivity to hyperparameters observed in ablations (Tables 4-6)
Gap between theory (assumes optimal discriminator, absolute continuity conditions) and practice (finite adversarial training, conditions never verified); no quantification of approximation error
Cell tracking evaluation is purely qualitative (acknowledged: 'results in mentioned figures are conclusive'); quantitative metrics available but not used
Spatial transcriptomics validated on single dataset only; limited generalization claims; no multiple ST datasets
Computational costs not compared; no wall-clock time analysis; added complexity (GAN + CFM two-stage training) vs. simpler baselines unjustified
Regularizer selection unclear for practitioners; three proposed regularizers used differently across experiments (linear for knot, piecewise-linear for ST, second-derivative for scRNA)
Limited baseline comparison fairness: dismissal of MFM time-dependent variants conflates algorithm with tuning; OT-MFM with time-independent LAND sometimes performs reasonably
Incomplete statistical testing; error bars overlap in several comparisons despite claimed improvements
Reproducibility concerns: no mention of code availability, manual spatial alignment introduces subjectivity, extensive hyperparameter tuning not fully documented

strengths: Clear problem motivation identifying limitations of existing multi-marginal FM methods and proposing a conceptually novel distribution-matching approach
Theoretical contributions with formal uniqueness theorems (2.1, 2.2) and proofs providing guarantees for regularised interpolation problems
Comprehensive experimental scope across four diverse applications (synthetic knot, cell tracking, scRNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics) with detailed hyperparameter specifications
Strong qualitative results on challenging cases with non-smooth geometry and large K; visual demonstration of smoother interpolants than piecewise baselines
Novel application to spatial transcriptomics with meaningful improvements (EMD 98.91 vs 109.76-183.88 for baselines)
Well-presented paper with extensive appendices providing implementation details and ablation studies
weaknesses: Mixed empirical results: on scRNA-seq (largest validation), method performs on par with OT-MFM rather than superior; authors acknowledge this limitation stating 'difficult to completely outperform OT-MFM'
Lack of quantitative metrics on key experiments: synthetic knot and cell tracking validation rely only on visual inspection; no EMD or similar metrics despite having ground truth

Incremental novelty: straightforward application of established adversarial training techniques to multi-marginal FM; theoretical uniqueness results are direct applications of optimal transport theory without conceptual innovation

Insufficient treatment of GAN challenges: no convergence guarantees for min-max optimization, no mode collapse analysis, limited sensitivity analysis for discriminator architecture, and no principled guidance for regulariser selection across datasets

Methodological concerns: two-stage training with error propagation not analysed; unfair baseline comparisons with varying preprocessing and hyperparameter tuning; different regularisers used across experiments without clear selection criteria
Scalability claims unsupported: high-dimensional experiments (50D, 100D) show no improvement over baselines; 1200-marginal experiment uses only 2D synthetic data; computational cost not reported

Spatial transcriptomics results limited to single dataset with only K=4 sections and leave-one-out evaluation on 2 sections; improvements could be dataset-specific rather than demonstrating general superiority

Missing ablations on key design choices: alternative GAN objectives (Wasserstein, R3GAN mentioned but not systematically compared); sensitivity to discriminator architecture; effect of coupling choice beyond Fig. 9 appendix comparison

strengths: Novel conceptual approach: Using adversarial learning to match intermediate marginals in distribution (rather than pointwise) is genuinely innovative and addresses a real limitation of existing methods
Strong empirical results on spatial transcriptomics: Clear improvement over baselines (EMD: 98.91±2.03 vs 109.76±9.98 for OT-CFM), demonstrating clear utility in at least one important application
Handles challenging data regimes well: Demonstrates scalability to many marginals (1200 synthetic marginals), noisy data (cell tracking), and time-varying geometry with smooth interpolants
Theoretical grounding: Provides uniqueness theorems (2.1, 2.2) for learned interpolants under regularization, adding rigor to the approach
Comprehensive evaluation: Diverse experiments spanning synthetic, cell tracking, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomics data with extensive implementation details in appendices
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with good motivation and clear exposition of methodology, making contributions accessible
weaknesses: Mixed empirical results on standard benchmarks: On single-cell trajectory inference, performance is comparable or sometimes worse than baselines (Table 2: 48.496±0.814 vs 42.232±0.249 for OT-MFM at 100D), suggesting method is specialized rather than universally superior
Incomplete quantitative evaluation: Cell tracking experiments (§4.2) lack quantitative metrics despite being standard; justification that 'results are conclusive' is insufficient for reproducibility

GAN training complexity: Requires careful tuning of architecture choices (R3GAN for single-cell vs standard GAN elsewhere), multiple regularizer options, learning rates, and noise injection; no systematic stability analysis provided
Unfair experimental comparisons: Baseline difficulties undermine conclusions (MFM had NaN numerical issues requiring special handling; OT-CFM diverged so couldn't be quantitatively evaluated)
No computational cost analysis: Missing timing comparisons and computational complexity analysis despite potential overhead from 70,000-epoch ALI pretraining and GAN objectives

Theory-practice gap: Uniqueness theorems assume exact marginal matching (Eq. 6), but GAN only achieves approximate matching; connection unclear. Theorems rely on standard OT results with limited conceptual novelty

Limited guidance on method selection: Three regularizers proposed with unclear selection criteria; ablation results are unintuitive (increasing λ with piecewise linear regularizer worsens performance)
Missing details: Unspecified step-size h in numerical differentiation (Eq. 16), unclear OT solver choice, and which computational bottlenecks exist
